name: Barclays
title: Barclays offers a golden lesson in how not to handle a return-to-office mandate
description:
Barclays’ public retreat over its return-to-office policy reveals how even well-intentioned management decisions can backfire when employees are told what to do without understanding why.
Over the summer and September, Barclays has run through a sequence familiar to anyone who has watched a change programme stall.
Barclays had cited collaboration and working together; banks including JP Morgan and Revolut have argued that remote working harms the training of younger staff.
Asked why senior staff should attend four days rather than three, Barclays said the extra day would “support collaboration, decision-making and leadership visibility“.
Marcus Iles is a business strategy and organisational behaviour expert specialising in strategy activation, leadership alignment, organisational storytelling and people engagement.
text:
Barclays’ public retreat over its return-to-office policy reveals how even well-intentioned management decisions can backfire when employees are told what to do without understanding why. Marcus Iles says that if leaders want lasting change rather than reluctant compliance, they must build a shared sense of purpose

In the summer, Barclays told its UK staff that from October 5 most staff coming into the office two days a week would need to come in at least three, and that managing directors and above would need four. On September 29, with six days to go, the bank’s executive committee wrote to staff that it was “extending the implementation period for UK colleagues to ensure colleagues have the right support as we move through the transition”, and that it was “also reviewing our flexible working policy”. Employees could defer compliance until 2027 if their line manager agreed by the end of the week. On the same day a spokesperson told the press: “Our updated onsite working arrangements will take effect as planned.” Barclays’ public statement also acknowledged transitional measures for staff whose personal circumstances prevented them from meeting the requirements.

It would be easy to read the episode as one more skirmish in the long war over remote working. I think, however, it’s more useful as a case study of a wider and considerably more expensive issue: what happens to a strategic decision when it’s issued as an instruction rather than built as a shared understanding.

Over the summer and September, Barclays has run through a sequence familiar to anyone who has watched a change programme stall. First instruction, then revolt, then renewed justification and finally the retreat-presented-as-continuity. Each stage followed from the one before, and all of it was avoidable from the beginning.

The approach I use with leadership teams starts from a simple observation. For people to act together on a strategy, three things have to be held in common. The first is attention: what we are looking at. The second is interpretation: what we think it means. The third is expectation: what we believe will happen next and what is now expected of us. A strategy that settles the first and neglects the other two is a demand that people lack the shared understanding to execute.

Consider the instruction. The policy specified days more clearly than it explained why those days were necessary. Barclays had cited collaboration and working together; banks including JP Morgan and Revolut have argued that remote working harms the training of younger staff. But citing those benefits did not explain why they required this particular number of days. And when an organisation supplies a number without a meaning, its people supply the meaning themselves. On Reddit, one commenter suggested that the bank wanted to justify money spent on refurbished buildings. Although that may be unfair, it’s a clear example of what a gap in shared interpretation produces: the most cynical account available fills any space that leadership leaves empty.

Then came the revolt. Thousands of staff signed an open letter drafted by Unite, which represents around 36,000 of the bank’s employees. It asks for a one-off payment before March 2027, childcare vouchers, subsidised meals, travel allowances and exemptions for anyone commuting more than 40 minutes. The letter described the effects of the policy as “material and foreseeable”. The union also asks for guaranteed weekly time for meaningful in-person work or team-building. The financial demands are the language of a transaction. When people have not accepted the reason for a decision, the conversation turns to what it will cost them and what they should be paid to bear it. The demands put a price on compliance without establishing a shared purpose. The letter recognises the value of face-to-face collaboration but disputes whether that requires a blanket increase in attendance.

The justification repeated during the dispute is the most informative step for us observers. Asked why senior staff should attend four days rather than three, Barclays said the extra day would “support collaboration, decision-making and leadership visibility“. Collaboration and decision-making are purposes, but visibility is not – it’s a condition. To be visible is to be seen, which is not the same as being available, being useful or teaching anyone anything. Anniken Grønstad, an associate professor of organisational psychology at Oslo New University College, drew the distinction precisely in a recent interview with Science Norway: if an experienced employee “sits behind a closed door or spends large parts of the day in meetings,” she said, “the main thing the younger employees have gained is a shorter physical distance to a potential mentor. They don’t necessarily have better access to the mentor’s expertise.” Her conclusion belongs in front of any board weighing a mandate: “the office itself is not the training model”.

‘Leadership visibility’ is what an organisation says when it has confused the observable with the consequential. I suspect it is also what many staff believed the policy was about all along. Gallup research published last month bears on this directly. Among surveyed workers in the United States, 59 per cent believe their employer collects activity data such as hours worked and badge swipes. Only 19 per cent say someone at work has spoken to them about the data or metrics collected about their work. Among employees who regularly work on a computer or another device, only 20 per cent trust their leaders “a great deal” to use that data responsibly. Being counted without being told why is a reliable way to persuade people that the counting is the point.

Which brings us to the retreat. The concession is real, if partial: deferral to 2027 for those whose managers allow it, and a review of flexible working. The public insistence that the arrangements would take effect as planned sits uneasily with the extension offered to colleagues. Barclays is, in effect, telling two audiences two stories and trusting that neither will compare notes. Yet they already have. One self-identified Barclays employee asked why they were still being told to return three days a week from Monday. Others read the delay as postponing the inevitable, or speculated that resignations had forced the bank’s hand.

There is a further, quieter consequence. By routing deferrals through individual line managers, Barclays has turned one leadership decision into thousands of local ones. Each will be made a little differently. Each will be read by the person on the receiving end as a verdict on how far their manager trusts them. A policy meant to bring people together now risks sorting them, team by team, into the accommodated and the refused. It is a lottery, and lotteries do not build cohesion.

None of this means Barclays is wrong to want its people together more often. There are serious arguments for in-person work, especially early in a career, and the bank’s own statements acknowledge “the benefits of balancing flexibility for colleagues with the importance of working together”. But stating the argument did not establish a shared understanding with the people expected to act on it. Grønstad notes that managers’ claims about learning, creativity and knowledge transfer in the office are empirical claims, and should therefore be backed up with evidence. I’d go further. Even well-evidenced claims do nothing until people share an understanding of what they require.

What would that have looked like? Not, I would argue, a better communications plan. The work starts earlier, and it follows a sequence. First, leaders must listen to the stories that will already be circulating in and about the organisation, before a decision is announced. The story about expensive refurbished buildings was presumably not invented in September. Then, leaders must shape a reason that people can understand and act on. That reason should then be shared and opened to challenge, so that “material and foreseeable” costs surface as design problems rather than grievances. The next step is to check whether leaders’ own behaviour fits the account they are giving. This is where ‘leadership visibility’ was always going to fail, because visibility is something done to others, not with them. When leaders’ behaviours are aligned to an authentic, meaningful story they’ve developed with colleagues, a real shift in behaviour follows. Returning to the story as circumstances change then enables leaders to sustain the strategy, rather than defending the original number.

The cost of skipping this work rarely shows up in the policy itself but, instead, later as compliance that does not deliver the intended outcome. Barclays may well get its people into the building three days a week by 2027. But what it certainly won’t get, without a shared account of why, is whatever it wanted those days for.

It’s an important reminder that while proximity can be mandated, meaning cannot.

Marcus Iles is a business strategy and organisational behaviour expert specialising in strategy activation, leadership alignment, organisational storytelling and people engagement. With 25 years’ experience spanning advertising, creative strategy, organisational storytelling and consultancy, Marcus – a former Chief Storytelling Officer at The Storytellers and an award-winning advertising creative and strategist – examines why strategies that appear clear at leadership level can fragment when they are interpreted and acted upon across an organisation.

The US grocer has battled cautious consumer spending, particularly ​by lower-income shoppers, as food and fuel costs climb, alongside market share ‌loss to mass retailers such as Walmart, discount chains and private-label brands.

The review builds on a restructuring, announced in July, and is expected to be completed in the fourth quarter ending February 2027.

By then, Albertsons also aims to provide fresh short- and long-term financial targets alongside a “comprehensive turnaround plan”.

“We must turn ‌things ​around,” Meg Whitman, the former eBay and Hewlett-Packard CEO ⁠who was named executive chair last ⁠month in a newly created role to help the grocer “sharpen its strategy and strengthen execution”, said on a post-earnings call.

The company needs to move faster to cut costs and reinvest much of those savings to lower prices and improve store ​experience, she said.

CEO Susan Morris said Albertsons had accumulated too many initiatives, processes and layers of complexity over time, slowing the organization and increasing costs.

“We’re not satisfied with ⁠the results and the current trajectory of our ⁠business,” she said.

The expanded turnaround effort comes nearly two years after ​Albertsons’ proposed $24.6 billion merger with Kroger collapsed after a federal court blocked the deal on ​antitrust grounds. Albertsons subsequently terminated the agreement.

The company’s shares rose 2% on ‌Tuesday, reversing premarket losses. They had fallen 27% so far this year.

“They have hard time remaining competitive on price as some mass merchants such as Walmart have used grocery as a traffic driver and have other high margin categories such as fashion to offset ⁠food’s low margins,” said Bruce Winder, an independent retail consultant.

In July, Albertsons outlined plans to expand private-label offerings and improve e-commerce, while restructuring its 11 divisions into four regions and ⁠centralizing merchandising.

Albertsons on Tuesday described ‌those changes as the first step in its broader turnaround.

“We’ll ⁠exit areas that are underperforming,” Morris said on Tuesday.

text:
Advances Agilent's position as a leading pathology solutions provider, with a unique and differentiated combination of instruments, reagents, and software

Acquisition seamlessly builds on Agilent's pathology portfolio expansion efforts and widens strategic moat in high-growth market

SANTA CLARA, Calif. & PHILADELPHIA, October 13, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Agilent Technologies Inc. (NYSE: A) today announced it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Proscia®, a provider of digital pathology software for clinical and life-sciences customers, in an all-cash transaction valued at $240 million in cash at closing and up to an additional $30 million based on achieving future performance milestones.

Proscia is a leading independent provider of enterprise digital pathology software, serving as a key enabler to address emerging trends in the $5 billion Pathology market. Proscia's software platform serves as a central operating layer for digital pathology, supporting clinical and life-sciences customers across the U.S. and Europe. By connecting slide scanners, laboratory information systems, image-analysis applications, AI tools, people, and data, Proscia's innovative technology enables customers to manage images, data, and workflows in one unified environment. Proscia serves more than 4,000 laboratories, hospitals, and clinics today as well as 16 of the top 20 pharmaceutical companies, with trailing twelve months revenue exceeding $18 million. Proscia was named 2026 Best in KLAS for Digital Pathology and earned the highest performance score across both U.S. and European markets.

Agilent and Proscia entered into a multi-year distribution agreement in September 2022 to offer a comprehensive digital diagnostic-pathology system. Today's announcement builds on Agilent's established pathology solutions and its partnership with Proscia.

"Digital pathology is quickly becoming the foundation for pathology data generation, analysis, and application across biopharmaceutical research, clinical development, and diagnostics, and our acquisition of Proscia meaningfully expands our presence in this fast-growing market," said Agilent President and CEO Padraig McDonnell. "The acquisition establishes an Agilent platform for scientific intelligence in tissue-based precision medicine, connecting data generation with AI-based interpretation in a workflow that supports biomarker research through routine clinical use. With Proscia's leading platform and talented team, we will be better equipped to help laboratories and biopharma customers manage and derive insights from pathology data. We look forward to welcoming the Proscia team to Agilent and working together to accelerate adoption of AI-enabled pathology workflows to advance drug discovery and companion-diagnostics solutions and create long-term value for customers and shareholders."

"This agreement with Agilent marks an exciting milestone for Proscia and reflects the strength of the platform our team has built," said David West, Co-Founder and CEO of Proscia. "Agilent shares our vision for advancing pathology through open, digital, and AI-enabled solutions. Together, we can accelerate innovation while continuing to provide customers with the flexibility they need across clinical and life-sciences workflows. I am grateful to the entire Proscia team, whose dedication made this milestone possible, and look forward to building on our work as part of Agilent."

Strategic and Financial Benefits of the Acquisition

The combination builds on the successful completion of Agilent's recent transaction with Biocare Medical, and offers meaningful strategic and financial benefits, including:

Strengthens Pathology Portfolio with a Leading Digital Pathology Platform. This acquisition strengthens Agilent's existing leadership in pathology instrumentation and reagents, combining industry-leading diagnostic capabilities with Proscia's vendor-agnostic digital pathology platform and established customer base. Proscia's platform holds FDA 510(k) clearance for primary diagnosis. The transaction builds on Agilent's position as a leader in pathology, well-positioning the Company to address evolving customer needs as the market embraces digitalization and AI.

Enhances Companion Diagnostics and Biopharma Drug Discovery Offerings. By leveraging a growing repository of real-world data, Proscia offers additional AI-enabled synergies with Agilent's companion diagnostics (CDx) business, enhancing value to biopharma partners as well as clinical and translational research customers.

Supports Agilent's Long-Term Growth Profile. Proscia's recurring-revenue model will add a high-growth, high-margin software business to Agilent's pathology portfolio.

The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions and is expected to close early in Agilent's fiscal year 2027. Upon closing, Proscia will become part of the Agilent Life Sciences and Diagnostics Markets Group.

Advisers

DLA Piper LLP (US) is serving as legal adviser and Joele Frank is serving as strategic communications adviser to Agilent.

Cooley LLP is serving as legal adviser to Proscia.

About Agilent Technologies

Agilent Technologies, Inc. (NYSE: A) is a global leader in analytical and clinical laboratory technologies, delivering insights and innovation that help our customers bring great science to life. Agilent's full range of solutions includes instruments, software, services, and expertise that provide trusted answers to our customers' most challenging questions. The company generated revenue of $6.95 billion in fiscal year 2025 and employs approximately 18,000 people worldwide. Information about Agilent is available at www.agilent.com. To receive the latest Agilent news, subscribe to the Agilent Newsroom. Follow Agilent on LinkedIn and Facebook.

Proscia is the pathology AI company rewiring pathology for precision medicine across drug discovery, development, and diagnosis. Its Concentriq platform brings intelligence to the scientists, pathologists, and laboratory leaders behind the most critical decisions in medicine, helping more breakthroughs reach the patients they were made for. Proscia is trusted by 16 of the top 20 pharmaceutical companies and was named Global 2026 Best in KLAS for Digital Pathology in Europe. text:
OpenAI has announced a $1 billion commitment to help cyber defenders protect essential services, including water systems, electricity networks, local government services and community banks.

The initiative, Daybreak for Frontline Defenders, will give organizations with limited security resources subsidized access to OpenAI’s advanced cybersecurity tools, alongside training, technical assistance and partnerships. OpenAI is targeting the subsidized access to be consumed over the next six months, beginning in the United States before expanding to partner countries.

The commitment addresses a practical problem for many essential-service providers: small security teams are responsible for protecting complex, aging systems against increasingly capable attackers.

OpenAI says its tools can help those teams review older software, analyze suspicious activity, identify vulnerabilities, prioritize risks and develop and test fixes.

In a LinkedIn announcement, OpenAI for Government wrote: “We depend on cyber defenders to protect the systems that keep communities running: the water coming from the tap, the electricity powering homes and businesses, the local government systems that deliver public services, and the financial institutions people trust with their money.”

Subsidized access for teams with limited resources

The US element, Daybreak for America, will prioritize water and wastewater systems, electricity grid operators, state and local governments, community and regional banks, nonprofits and open-source software maintainers.

The $1 billion commitment is for subsidized access to Daybreak, rather than a cash grant fund distributed to participating organizations.

OpenAI says the initiative builds on support offered following recent attacks on US water systems. Affected states and utilities were offered up to $1 million in no-cost application programming interface credits, Daybreak access and technical assistance.

According to the company, participating teams used that support to review software and system settings, validate security findings, develop patches and confirm fixes while water services remained operational.

Daybreak provides different levels of access for verified defenders carrying out authorized security work. Daybreak Blue supports common defensive tasks using OpenAI’s mainline models, while Daybreak Red gives approved organizations access to specialized models for more sensitive and technically demanding work.

OpenAI reports that thousands of defenders across 2,000 approved organizations and workspaces already use the program.

Training and a public-sector pilot

A new pilot with the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center, known as MS-ISAC, will pair Daybreak access with guided training and hands-on assistance for an initial group of public-sector and water-system defenders.

The work will help participating teams check and prioritize findings, coordinate fixes and develop an approach that can be repeated across other organizations.

MS-ISAC provides threat intelligence, incident-response support and shared security services to public-sector organizations. Its wider membership includes utilities, public hospitals, schools and law-enforcement agencies.

The initial announcement focuses on public-sector and water-system defenders. It does not confirm a separate rollout for schools.

OpenAI is also holding meetings with frontline teams to understand how they can use its tools. The company says its second gathering of utility providers included participants representing 40 states and the District of Columbia, collectively serving more than half the US population.

Moving from finding weaknesses to fixing them

More than 35 partner products and partner-operated services are being announced through the Daybreak Defense Network, bringing OpenAI’s cybersecurity models into tools and services that security teams already use.

The company has also published its approach to a “Defense Factory,” an operation that uses AI agents alongside existing security and engineering tools to find and validate vulnerabilities and prepare tested fixes for human review.

The emphasis is on helping organizations act on security findings. Access to a capable model still needs to be accompanied by the expertise, processes and support required to deploy fixes safely.

OpenAI says it intends to expand the subsidized-access model to partner countries in the coming weeks. Eligible governments, critical infrastructure operators, nonprofits, open-source maintainers and supporting organizations can find information about access, training and technical assistance through the Daybreak website.

text:
At the end of 2025, Delta Air Lines announced plans to launch a flashy and unconventional route for a U.S. carrier by October of the following year.

The new flight between Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport (ATL) in Atlanta and Riyadh King Khalid International Airport (RUH) will be the first direct service to Saudi Arabia for any U.S. airline.

The decision to expand into the Middle Eastern nation came amid rising tourism numbers and the latter country's efforts to grow its tourism industry to rival that of nearby Dubai in the United Arab Emirates, as well as overcome its past reputation as a closed-off country.

Almost all of that plan was completely upended when the joint U.S.-Israeli strike on Iran in February 2026 threw the entire Middle Eastern region into turmoil that continues to spill over far beyond the site of the original attack.

Delta Air Lines confirms delay of much-hyped Atlanta-Riyadh flight

In the most recent escalation, a series of cruise missile strikes that the Islamist paramilitary Houthi group launched on Saudi Arabia's main airport on Oct. 10 killed 13 travelers and injured hundreds of others.

The ongoing risk of follow-up strikes on the airport remains high. For example, a second strike on Oct. 13 killed one and injured 11, according to the BBC.

Most international airlines have suspended flights into Riyadh until at least November, in some cases pushing the restart of service to 2027.

Related: Airport shut down, international airlines cancel flights after Houthi attack

Although European carriers such as KLM are still hoping to resume their own service into Riyadh by November, Delta Air Lines has now confirmed that it is pushing back the launch of its Atlanta-Riyadh route until March 2027.

The closure of King Khalid International to flights was also recently extended until Oct. 17.

Delta delays launch of nonstop service from Atlanta to Riyadh

"Delta will delay the planned launch of its nonstop service between Atlanta and Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, amid evolving developments in the region," the airline said in its statement.

"The safety and security of our customers and employees always come first and continue to guide our operational decisions. We remain in close contact with relevant government and aviation partners, including Saudia and Riyadh Air, as we monitor the situation."

More Travel News:

Airline to launch unusual new flight to Cayman Islands from the U.S.

There is a very cool Irish version of swimming pigs in The Bahamas

Unexpected country is most luxurious travel destination for 2026

Low-cost airline launches easier way to get to Sri Lanka

The suspension is surely a disappointment to passengers who already booked travel and to the airline itself, given how much it touted the route before the original launch date.

Passengers who booked the Atlanta-Riyadh flight will receive communication from the airline about options for rescheduling or obtaining a refund.

Delta confirmed that travelers whose fare class otherwise would otherwise not allow for it will be able to receive a refund to their original method of payment.

"Saudi Arabia remains an important market for Delta, and we are committed to serving the Kingdom for the long-term," Delta said of the route suspension. "We look forward to connecting Saudi Arabia to Delta's global network in March 2027."

title: BNY Expands Digital Asset Custody Platform in Europe Through MiCA-Registered Entity
description:
Financial giants including Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) and Standard Chartered are expanding their digital asset custody businesses.
Launched in 2022, BNY’s Digital Asset Custody platform provides institutional clients with infrastructure to securely hold and service digital assets.
With its European expansion, BNY is extending its existing asset servicing capabilities into the regulated digital asset markets of Europe.
Growing Digital Asset Custody Business The move marks another major push by a traditional finance giant into digital asset custody as institutional demand for regulated crypto infrastructure grows.
According to Fortune Business Insights, the global digital asset custody market can reach $2.88 trillion by 2034.
text:
Wall Street’s crypto custody race is heating up. Financial giants including Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) and Standard Chartered are expanding their digital asset custody businesses. Now, BNY is the latest traditional finance heavyweight to strengthen its position in the sector.

In its latest move, BNY has announced the expansion of its digital asset custody platform in Europe, under the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) framework.

Announced on October 8, the move gives select institutional clients access to regulated cryptocurrency custody services in Europe. It follows BNY’s European banking entity, The Bank of New York Mellon SA/NV, being added to the European Securities and Markets Authority’s (ESMA) MiCA register in July 2026.

The expansion comes shortly after Standard Chartered announced plans to expand its digital asset custody in Singapore. It builds onto the going acceleration on how major banking institutions are building infrastructure to serve growing demand for crypto custody, stablecoins and tokenized financial assets.

BNY’s move is particularly significant given its scale in traditional finance. As of June 30, 2026, the bank oversaw $62.6 trillion in assets under custody and/or administration and managed $2.2 trillion in assets.

What Is BNY’s Digital Asset Custody Platform?

Launched in 2022, BNY’s Digital Asset Custody platform provides institutional clients with infrastructure to securely hold and service digital assets. It uses multiparty computation technology, segregated client wallets and private-key security controls to protect assets.

The platform supports institutional access to Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), Solana (SOL) and USDC. It also has plans to expand its range of supported crypto assets and stablecoins.

With its European expansion, BNY is extending its existing asset servicing capabilities into the regulated digital asset markets of Europe. It will be giving eligible institutions another route to access crypto custody through an established banking partner.

As per its official press release, the bank’s broader digital assets strategy also extends beyond cryptocurrencies. BNY is also exploring how custody infrastructure can support tokenized securities, digital payments, settlement and collateral management as traditional financial institutions increasingly assess onchain applications.

Growing Digital Asset Custody Business

The move marks another major push by a traditional finance giant into digital asset custody as institutional demand for regulated crypto infrastructure grows. According to Fortune Business Insights, the global digital asset custody market can reach $2.88 trillion by 2034. BNY’s European expansion comes amid a broader push by major banks to establish a foothold in the sector, with Standard Chartered also expanding its digital asset custody operations. The push comes as crypto native companies like Bitgo continuing to build on the digital custody infrastructure.

NYSE Parent ICE is also eyeing $184B Crypto ETF Custody market with its separate entity Digital Trust.

Interestingly, while BNY and Standard Chartered do not separately disclose profits from crypto custody, digital asset infrastructure provider BitGo reported $77.4 million in subscription and services revenue in 2024, according to its SEC filings. The segment includes institutional wallet and custody solutions, although the company does not break out custody revenue separately.

Thus. the expansion by major banks signals a growing focus on building regulated infrastructure to serve institutional clients entering digital asset markets.

text:
The agreement marks an important step in the industrial roll-out of Perpetual Next’s Biomethanol Blueprint, a standardised concept designed to enable the serial development and replication of large-scale biomethanol facilities based on proven industrial technologies.

Under the Agreement, Air Liquide Engineering and Technologies will provide their Rectisol and Lurgi Methanol technology. The technology is designed to process syngas from a broad range of sources, including syngas from biomass and has been deployed in numerous industrial plants worldwide.

Perpetual Next’s Blueprint integrates torrefaction, gasification, syngas cleaning and upgrade, with methanol synthesis to convert low-grade organic waste, including waste wood, into biomethanol. The standardised approach is intended to reduce development complexity, support repeatable project execution and create economies of scale across a portfolio of facilities.

The company is developing its biomethanol portfolio to address growing demand for renewable carbon-based methanol in the chemical industry and maritime sector. Its Delfzijl facility in the Netherlands is planned with an annual biomethanol production capacity of 220,000 tonnes, while the company’s broader global development pipeline is intended to create significant production capacity through replication of the Blueprint.

“This suite of agreements marks an important milestone in the industrialisation of our Biomethanol Blueprint” said Rolf Bosma, Managing Director, Perpetual Next. “Delfzijl will be the first application of the concept, providing the foundation for subsequent projects in Moerdijk, Poland, Estonia and other sites worldwide. By establishing a framework with Air Liquide for multiple biomethanol sites, we are creating a scalable technology platform that supports the roll-out of our biomethanol portfolio.”

The agreement combines Perpetual Next’s standardised project concept and feedstock strategy with Air Liquide’s established technology and engineering capabilities, providing a platform for the development of multiple industrial-scale biomethanol facilities.

title: How the weight loss market is prompting pharma biggies to look at India afresh
description:

text:
Additionally, the India centre has developed new systems and processes that are shared with other centres and are being adopted globally. “In this, India is really a peer to our US and European centres, particularly for clinical trials,” says Ricks.

Fat is the fuel

Eli Lilly has been in India for more than three decades. Ricks says this is the company’s fourth or fifth push in the country. Earlier efforts—including a 1993 partnership with Ranbaxy, once India’s largest pharma company which eventually passed into the hands of Sun Pharma, and launches in areas such as oncology and antibiotics—failed to gain enough traction. Lilly did not have products to reach large sections of the population.

It is different this time, because of the burgeoning weight loss drugs market, whose buoyancy is making global pharma giants such as Lilly and Novo look at India afresh. It is no longer merely a large market for cheaper, generic versions of the drugs MNCs spend billions to develop, or a country where they delay introducing their new drugs for as long as possible and then bear in stoic silence the loss of revenue as generic versions rush in.

India is now also a hub of drug development for them and may become one of manufacturing as well. Lilly last year committed $1 billion to expand its contract manufacturing network here. Novo, the Danish pharma giant that competes with Lilly globally, shares its rival’s sentiments.

“In the obesity space also, we have always had a very strong development presence in India,” Novo’s executive vice-president of R&D and chief scientific officer, Martin Hoist Lange, said in an interview with Forbes India in late September. “So, a good proportion of our clinical trials is with people from India. Thereby also obliging ourselves to launch our products in India and making our products available for people in India. So, from an R&D perspective, India is an integral part of how we do our development.”

Lilly is setting up a joint laboratory with an Indian partner, whose name it has not yet disclosed, focused on process development work. At the same time, it is working with Indian manufacturers to produce registered starting materials and other key ingredients used in some of its biggest products, including its weight loss blockbuster Mounjaro. The move is part of a broader effort to diversify supply chains.

“We have all become concerned that we were over relying on one country for these,” says Ricks. Establishing an Indian base for critical inputs, he adds, has become strategically important. About a year into the effort, “it is going really well”.

For now, Lilly’s manufacturing footprint in India remains export-oriented. But that could change as the demand grows. “We tend to locate our manufacturing plants near our largest markets. So far, India has not been a large market. But as India grows, we’ll need to produce more, and we can look at production close to the market here,” says Ricks.

Indeed, everyone likes to have their development and manufacturing bases as close to their largest markets as possible. That is one box ticked with the India market getting fattened by weight loss drugs. The other factor, the unexpected catalyst, is artificial intelligence, or AI, which is changing the mechanics of pharma research.

In a blog titled, ‘We Must Pace the Frontier’, Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei says: “I believe that AI could cure most major diseases in the next 5–10 years.”

Might of weight loss

In March 2025, Eli Lilly launched Mounjaro in India. By October, it had become the country’s top‑selling drug by value overtaking the long‑standing market leader, GSK’s Augmentin. In June 2025, Novo entered the fray with Wegovy, its obesity‑focused semaglutide injection, and launched the much-awaited Ozempic in India in December.

Both Ozempic and Mounjaro make you feel full sooner and for longer. But Mounjaro, which was approved five years after Ozempic and whose chemical name is tirzepatide, acts on both GLP-1 and GIP receptors. These are specialised proteins found on the surface of cells and play an important role in how the human body processes energy. Ozempic, whose chemical name is semaglutide, works only on GLP-1.

India’s weight loss drugs category is estimated to have risen to ₹2,300 crore from ₹750 crore a year prior, largely driven by semaglutide going off patent on March 20, 2026, which saw 23 Indian generic versions of it launched within 24 hours.

“It is inevitable,” says Ricks. “That is a by-product of our industry.” He however adds that the flood of generics has not affected Mounjaro’s growth. Instead, he says, “It has brought more people into the market.”

These would be people inclined towards weight loss drugs but daunted by their high prices. “This is part of the normal cycle of our business,” he says. The same thing happened in Brazil and Canada.

How does an inventor company convince buyers to pay more for their medicines despite the presence of cheaper generics?

“Starting mostly with the physicians...,” says Ricks. “Through physicians we communicate… The clinical trials we have conducted… That if they are given a choice, what is the best alternative for people with obesity, people with diabetes… Now we have cardiovascular data that shows heart protection… And point out those differences when they are recommending something to a patient. I think we have comprehensive evidence versus semaglutide that is pretty convincing to most trained doctors.”

Now everything in that market needs to be assessed all over again, because the next big thing is round the corner. The market that has so far been injectables is about to receive its first dose of pills.

Beyond the needle

Oral GLP-1 pills are expected to come to India in the first half of 2027.

“It is always helpful to be the first,” says Ricks. “But in the case of cardio metabolic health, it seems less important because these are chronic medications, and often the best one rises to the top. We saw that in the injectable market.”

With the pills coming into the market, the fear is they will cannibalise injectables. There are use cases for both. Pills work well for patients who don’t want to inject themselves and those who prefer lower prices. Clinical studies by Eli Lilly show that in order to maintain a certain weight over time, patients can either lower the dose of Mounjaro or switch to Foundayo, which is Lilly’s oral GLP-1.

The differentiation between Lilly and Novo’s products boils down to chemistry. Ricks says Mounjaro (tirzepatide) has achieved massive success partly because it mimics two hormones released by the gut after a meal, helping regulate appetite and blood sugar. Novo’s semaglutide, sold as Ozempic for type 2 diabetes and Wegovy for obesity, works as a GLP-1 receptor. “The basic biology works a similar way. We have a lot of respect for our competitor,” says Ricks.

Novo’s oral semaglutide is a peptide—a short chain of amino acids—which brings its own formulation challenges: Ensuring the drug survives digestion and is absorbed into the bloodstream.

Lilly took a different approach with orforglipron (Foundayo), using a small chemical compound rather than a chain of amino acids (peptides) to activate the GLP-1 receptor. Ricks says this approach was more challenging scientifically but made production easier to scale up.

Novo’s Lange did not reveal when his company’s weight loss pill will come to India, but emphasised that Wegovy was the only drug in the obesity space that had an established cardiovascular risk reduction, by 20 percent, and a liver risk reduction. “And those benefits are also seen with the Wegovy pill,” he said.

He highlighted his drug’s benefits over its rival’s. “We have competitors that are in the subcutaneous space also give 21 percent weight loss at the highest dose. They don’t have the cardiovascular and liver benefits. They have a small molecule GLP-1 as a tablet. But that only gives 12 percent weight loss,” said Lange.

The Wegovy pill has been launched first in the US where it has an 85 percent share of the weight loss tablet market. “And we are slowly but surely launching outside of the US. So far, we have launched in three countries outside of the US, with the next being Mexico,” he said.

After weight loss

Both Lilly and Novo are betting on differentiated therapies as they expand their India portfolios.

Beyond weight loss drugs, Lilly plans to bring medicines to India across therapies. But for that it must grapple with standards that are not the same as the international benchmarks for registration, including local data and local clinical trials. “Doing clinical trials in India is more complicated than other markets. So, we are working with the government to streamline that,” says Ricks.

Dementia currently affects 8.8 million people in India, and it is expected to inflict 16.9 million by 2036. In May 2026, Eli Lilly launched its Alzheimer’s drug Kisunla (donanemab), also known as Lormalzi in India. It costs ₹91,688 for a 350-mg vial, which needs to be taken as an intravenous infusion once every four weeks.

This, in a price sensitive market, is expensive, made even more so by the wafer-thin health insurance coverage in the country which translates into patients paying out of their own pockets. Lilly says all its medicines are priced as per the GDP per capita of a country. “While Kisunla and Mounjaro may still seem expensive relative to their generic alternatives, there is a pretty big discount relative to the European or US pricing,” says Ricks. “That’s how we fund our research and development.”

Novo is excited about a new molecule called setagantide, which during Phase II trials showed 24 percent weight loss in 36 weeks and is now in Phase III. However, it too is awake to other opportunities in India. “From a commercial perspective, we intend to launch our products in India. It goes beyond obesity. In India, we are in diabetes, blood disorders, haemophilia, and sickle cell disease,” said Lange.

AI-Powered R&D

Amodei’s blog might suggest that the next breakthrough cancer medicine is a prompt away. “That,” Ricks says, “is not the case.”

Medicines live in the physical world. Innovator companies make a molecule that does not exist—a new chemical structure to interfere with biology. And it has to be safe. To prove a medicine’s efficacy and safety, it needs to be tested in people who have the disease. According to Ricks, there might only be a handful of medicines that can claim to be invented by AI and are in the human testing phase.

Lilly is deeply invested in AI for research and development, but in a different way.

Making early-stage drug research more efficient is one. Drawing on data from past laboratory experiments, Lilly’s models predict how a molecule might behave, how long it could remain active in the bloodstream, or whether it might cause unwanted effects. These predictions help scientists avoid spending time on candidates likely to fail, speeding up research and reducing costs.

In September 2025, the company launched Lilly TuneLab. It is a collaborative artificial intelligence and machine learning drug discovery platform. This gives smaller biotech companies free access to AI tools that can help them identify promising drug candidates.

Separately, Lilly has invested $1 billion with NVIDIA to build the largest biologic supercomputer in the world, called LillyPod. It is training AI models to predict human biology and eventually generate ideas for new drug programmes to help supercharge drug discovery. “It will take years to fully train models useful to scientists,” says Ricks.

Novo, in April, announced a partnership with OpenAI and in September it partnered with Anthropic. Both the partnerships are to embed advanced artificial intelligence across its entire drug development and operational pipeline.

“AI helps to amplify the volume and the speed, but it also helps by providing more insights and analysing the data that we generate. In the clinical space, it is also a huge productivity gain,” says Lange. Though AI can amplify and enable research, it cannot work in isolation. “We still need the human insights on top or in parallel with what we do with AI,” he adds.

text:
Andrea Orcel-led Italian banking giant UniCredit has sought EU antitrust approval for its takeover of the German bank Commerzbank, with regulators setting a November 16 deadline for their decision, according to a European Commission filing on Friday.

UniCredit’s two-year pursuit of acquiring Commerzbank, which faced intense opposition from the German lender and government, ultimately succeeded in July 2026, with Commerzbank entering into M&A talks with its Italian counterpart.

UniCredit, as of now, holds a total stake of 47.59% in Commerzbank (approximately 47.6%), which translates to 49.65% of the voting rights once treasury shares are cancelled.

European regulators, from their part, are backing cross-border mergers to create European banking champions.

The Commission, which is the EU competition enforcer, has two options as of now: either clear the deal with or ⁠without concessions during its preliminary review, or open a full-scale ⁠investigation if it has serious concerns.

Orcel, looking to take control of his acquisition target, is also eyeing the overhaul of the German lender’s supervisory board by as early ‌as January 2027.

As per the reports of the Financial Times, the Italian lender plans to call an extraordinary general meeting once it receives the remaining regulatory approvals needed to take control of Germany’s second-largest bank.

“UniCredit expects to secure control by the end of February and replace all 10 shareholder representatives on Commerzbank’s 20-member supervisory board, giving it an effective majority,” the media outlet stated in September.

While Berlin has softened its stance on a potential deal after UniCredit built a stake of nearly 50% in the German lender, Friedrich Merz has continued to demand that Commerzbank remain listed, keep its ⁠Frankfurt headquarters, and maintain its role in financing German medium-sized companies at home and abroad.

Germany won the right to appoint two board members ⁠when it rescued Commerzbank in 2009 during the global financial crisis. It retains a stake of 13.3% in the bank.

As per reports, Orcel wants sweeping changes at Commerzbank, including the departures of CEO Bettina Orlopp and Chairman Jens Weidmann.

Orlopp has, however, maintained a cooperative stance, proposing that Commerzbank could potentially acquire UniCredit’s German bank HVB in shares to create a mutually beneficial merger.

Orlopp, speaking at a financial conference during September, ⁠said such a deal structure was one of several “options on the table” as a way to increase UniCredit’s shareholding in Commerzbank.

Orlopp also said that the other ways to structure a deal include a ⁠simple merger between Commerzbank and UniCredit or by UniCredit making another offer to the remaining ⁠Commerzbank shareholders—”most likely with a premium”—to get its shareholding ⁠above 90%.

She concluded by stating that all three basic options are available.

text:
By Jacqueline Munis

Among Americans’ many concerns about data centers—from the constant humming sound to high electricity prices—heavy water consumption stands out. Residents of towns with data centers have reported contaminated water, low water pressure, and unauthorized siphoning, putting one of life’s essentials under threat.

Nvidia thinks it has the solution for that: its new server infrastructure.

The company announced on Monday that its newest AI servers will entirely use liquid cooling, a method that eliminates the need for air-cooling fans that rely on water.

Instead, heat will be dissipated by a liquid coolant made of water and propylene glycol that’s recirculated in a closed loop. The company says the system doesn’t need to draw in new water.

“We have eliminated massive amounts of power usage and pretty much all water usage,” Ali Heydari, Nvidia’s director of data center cooling and infrastructure, said in a statement.

In addition, the coolant can remain operational at temperatures of up to 45 °C or 113 °F, a much higher temperature than previous systems.

The move towards a more energy-efficient system comes as the United Nations predicted earlier this month that AI-related water consumption could equal the annual needs of 1.3 billion people by the end of the decade.

Meanwhile, Nvidia is not the only company working towards significantly reducing its water consumption. In August 2024, Microsoft announced that its new data centers will stop using water for cooling, saving more than 125 million liters of water per year per data center.

“The thing that’s exciting about what Nvidia announced is it shows really what’s possible in terms of pushing up this liquid input temperature to 45°C,” said Andrew A. Chien, a professor of computer science at the University of Chicago. “It’s super important to push it up, because in many cases it allows you to do that cooling, that exhausting of heat to the outside environment without running HVAC units, without running air conditioners. Because if it’s cool enough outside, you don’t need to.”

Chien directs the CERES Center for Unstoppable Computing. For the past 10 years, the center has studied how to make data centers more efficient and reduce their negative environmental impacts. A higher cooling temperature goes against conventional wisdom, he explained. The industry standard is 30°C, which requires much more air conditioning to maintain.

“The reason that they want to do this is that if you can cool the chips at a higher temperature, it becomes easier to vent that heat into the outside environment, because it’s a higher temperature supply, and heat flows downhill,” Chien said.

While he said zero water use is unrealistic, liquid cooling will significantly reduce the need for water. The catch is that these systems are expensive.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment on the costs of the systems or if the company will be retrofitting existing data centers with the technology.

The company estimates that a 50-megawatt hyperscale facility could save over $4 million a year in cooling-related energy and water costs by moving to liquid-cooled infrastructure.

“It is a direction that more people should be trying to get to, because it’ll reduce the total power consumption of these large data centers,” Chien said.

text:
This post was created in partnership with Best Buy Ads

Key takeaways

CTV turns passive watching into an interactive experience that brands can leverage.

Compared to linear TV, brands can react to cultural moments and respond faster with CTV ads.

The TV remote control lets viewers interact with ads, giving marketers unique data points and targeting capabilities.

Could CTV take a page from social and reinvent the legacy television ad-watching experience?

During an ADWEEK House Advertising HQ group chat co-hosted with Best Buy Ads, marketing leaders discussed how commerce-powered CTV is poised to reshape what was once passive consumer television-watching into a highly targeted, interactive experience that drives business outcomes for brands.

A new frontier in television-led shopping

Patrick Albano, chief revenue officer for Best Buy Ads, kicked off the discussion on connected TV with a bold statement.

“What you’re seeing now is actual sales information, actual consumer graphs that show what people like and what they might buy, and then applying that to television,” he said. “I think the things we’re talking about are really going to revolutionize the way people watch TV.”

Catherine Fanone, senior sales director at LG Ad Solutions, shared that her company partners with Best Buy Ads to connect TV storytelling with a deeper understanding of shopper and brand outcomes.

“Best Buy Ads bring the commerce intelligence while LG brings the scale, the attention, and a more advanced screen environment. Hopefully, we can help brands really understand more how television connects or contributes to the path to purchase,” Fanone said.

The final part of the equation is reaching consumers in new, innovative ways.

“It was really hard to be culturally relevant on TV previously because you had to think so far in advance for when this is going to air, and you couldn’t be reactive to something that’s happening in real time,” explained Ty Stafford, founder and CEO of Hello Party.

Now, brands can do that on TV just like they do on social, he added. “You can make something that’s polished and looks good and happens to also be culturally relevant. And very few people are taking advantage of that right now.”

The two-way power of the remote

Albano pointed out that in a vertical like consumer electronics, buying happens in refresh cycles (e.g., buying a new phone every two or three years, or a TV or laptop every five to seven years). Data and insights can help brands understand where a specific customer is on that journey so they can get the right messaging to that person.

“Who’s five or seven years away from purchase? Maybe that’s the branding audience. Or who’s a week away, and maybe that’s your sales audience,” Albano explained. “The onus is on us to help provide that data and make it palatable. But that’s never been available for TV advertising before.”

One important tool helping drive some of these insights is the remote control, explained Rob Aksman, president and co-founder of BrightLine.

“Now that TV can be interacted with using the remote control, there are additional data signals that never existed before,” Aksman shared. Unlike traditional TV that relies on Nielsen ratings to determine how many viewers saw something, now there are signals coming in with every single click of the remote, he continued.

Brands are theoretically able to track every click or interaction. “All of those data signals can just feed this brain and this engine for better targeting and knowing when to follow up,” said Aksman.

Ending repeated commercial overkill

Aksman and the other panelists touched on the frustration of seeing the same ad over and over during an hours-long streaming binge.

“Every commercial is just saying ‘hello, nice to meet you,’ as if you haven’t seen it 10 times before,” said Aksman. He hopes more brands start taking advantage of new capabilities that allow them to sequence creative and use multiple, personalized, and engaging versions where data informs the next ad. “All of that is possible now. It’s just a matter of upstreaming it and making it happen,” he said.

Best of all, added Miles Fisher, VP of global strategic advertising partnerships at Roku, it’s not only large legacy brands that can do this.

“There’s this awesome opportunity for growth marketers and small and medium-sized brands to actually win the attention economy on streaming and CTV with these interactive ads, performance and outcomes,” Fisher said. “As streaming gets more democratized, CPMs are becoming more approachable to brands.”

text:
Delta Air Lines, Inc. (NYSE:DAL) has cut its 2026 earnings forecast despite reporting record third-quarter revenue, as surging jet fuel prices continue to overwhelm strong travel demand and higher ticket prices. On October 9, the airline reduced its adjusted EPS guidance to $5.10-$5.60 from $6.50-$7.50, citing an expected $6 billion increase in annual fuel expenses. The revision highlights a difficult investment question: how much of Delta's premium revenue growth can translate into sustainable earnings while one of its largest operating costs remains elevated?

Third-quarter adjusted revenue increased 15.7% to approximately $17.6 billion, but adjusted EPS of $1.72 missed consensus expectations. Fuel expenses rose 62% to $4.1 billion, exceeding management's July forecast by more than $500 million, while adjusted operating margin declined to 9.4% from 11.1%. The results demonstrate that even substantial revenue growth cannot guarantee margin expansion when fuel costs increase faster than an airline's ability to recover them through pricing.

The stock has gained over 20% during the last 6-months, compared to a 33.88% gain for Insider Monkey Billionaire Index and +18.18% return for State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust.

Pixabay/Public Domain

Premium Revenue Is Providing Support, But Fuel Remains the Bigger Driver

Delta Air Lines, Inc. (NYSE:DAL) continues to benefit from its emphasis on premium travelers and loyalty-related revenue. Premium revenue increased 18% year-over-year in Q3, while loyalty-related revenue also grew 18%. Remuneration from its American Express partnership increased 15% and remains on track to exceed $9 billion for the year, providing an additional revenue stream beyond conventional passenger ticket sales.

However, the company's ability to offset fuel inflation remains limited. Delta Air Lines, Inc. (NYSE:DAL) expects jet fuel to average approximately $4.25 per gallon in Q4, compared with $3.61 in Q3, and management has acknowledged that prices could remain elevated for some time. Although the airline has benefited from higher fares and disciplined capacity growth, additional price increases could eventually weaken passenger demand, particularly among more price-sensitive travelers.

Delta's Monroe refinery near Philadelphia provides some protection, with management expecting more than $700 million in benefits during 2026. The facility allows the company to retain refining profits that can partially offset higher fuel costs, particularly when the spread between crude oil and refined products widens. Nevertheless, that benefit remains relatively small compared with the projected $6 billion annual fuel-cost increase, leaving operating profitability heavily exposed to energy prices.

The Valuation Depends on a Recovery in Unit Economics

Delta Air Lines, Inc. (NYSE:DAL) trades at approximately 15 times estimated 2026 earnings, a relatively modest multiple considering its premium customer base and diversified revenue streams. However, this valuation depends on the company's ability to recover margins despite elevated fuel costs. Consensus estimates anticipate a 6.36% EPS decline in 2026 before growth rebounds to 39.62% in 2027 and 30.62% in 2028. Its estimated P/E consequently falls from 15.07 times 2026 earnings to 8.26 times 2028 earnings, indicating that the apparent valuation discount depends heavily on the expected profitability recovery. Is Delta's premium business model enough to justify its valuation relative to United? See which airline stock looks more attractive.

The reduction in free cash flow guidance reinforces that uncertainty. Delta now expects approximately $2.5 billion in 2026 free cash flow, down from its previous $3 billion-$4 billion outlook, even as management continues targeting stronger long-term margins and balance-sheet improvement. Raymond James, Susquehanna, Bernstein, and Wells Fargo maintained positive ratings while adjusting their price targets ahead of earnings, reflecting confidence in underlying demand but concern about the duration of fuel-related pressure.

The revised outlook makes cash conversion an increasingly important consideration for investors, particularly given the gap between reported profitability and the cash available after capital expenditures. We previously examined whether Delta's cash flow is keeping pace with its earnings, a question that has become even more relevant following the airline's latest guidance reduction.

Institutional positioning has remained relatively constructive, with hedge-fund ownership increasing from 68 to 75 funds in Q2. Berkshire Hathaway increased its position by 44% to approximately 57.3 million shares, suggesting that some investors continued to favor Delta's longer-term earnings potential despite near-term industry headwinds.

The next test is whether Delta Air Lines, Inc. (NYSE:DAL) can sustain improvements in revenue per available seat mile while controlling nonfuel unit costs and preserving cash generation. Its premium offerings and refinery provide meaningful competitive advantages, but neither eliminates the industry's exposure to fuel volatility. At approximately 15 times estimated 2026 earnings, the stock could become attractive if fuel prices stabilize and operating margins recover. If elevated fuel costs persist, however, the earnings rebound embedded in consensus estimates may prove more difficult to achieve.

While we acknowledge the potential of DAL as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. And, you know, it's it's part of their move to, which which we've seen from Google and and Amazon as well, to reduce their dependence on uh what you get from uh Nvidia or AMD and ensure that they kind of have a top-down approach uh to their AI deployments from the silicon to the models, to the agents and so on.

Now, it doesn't mean that they're going to stop purchasing Nvidia chips or AMD chips or Intel chips for that matter. They still need those because their customers may want them. Uh and so what they're doing is they say that they're taking a more heterogeneous uh genius approach where they're going to offer multiple types of silicon options. They're going to offer their own AI services as well as third-party services and allow customers to have the choice that they want.

And that's something that we've seen uh kind of throughout uh the kind of tech industry when it went from uh uh on-premise computing to the cloud. We had seen a bunch of companies say, okay, you can take this deployment or that deployment. Uh different companies opted for different cloud providers, kind of a multi-cloud approach is what it's called. And I think that's what we're going to see here. But with regards to Microsoft's own chips, they do say that it will power a lot of their own software going forward, and that includes their own AI capabilities.

So it'll be really interesting to to see how many chips and and what kind of dependence they they build up for their own processors uh to kind of insulate themselves from a reliance on these third-party chips from Nvidia and AMD.
